Why Scoring Matters When Baking Sourdough Baguettes

When you bake a sourdough baguette, the score you make on the dough’s surface isn’t just a decorative flourish—it’s a critical step that controls how the loaf expands and curls during bake time. A clean, well‑placed cut allows steam to escape, prevents unwanted bursts, and creates that iconic golden, crisp crust. If you’ve ever pulled a baguette out of the oven only to see a sad, flattened loaf, the culprit was likely a missed or poorly executed score.

Gather Your Essentials: The 3‑in‑1 Sourdough Whisk Set

Before you touch the dough, make sure you have the right tools. The Sourdough Whisk Set: Danish Dough Whisk, Dough Scraper, Bread Scoring Lame is a compact kit that covers every need for a beginner sourdough baker. The whisk helps you fold the dough, the scraper keeps the surface smooth, and the lame—your scoring partner—makes precise, clean cuts. Having all three in one set saves space and keeps the workflow smooth.

Step‑by‑Step: How to Score Sourdough Baguettes

Follow these practical steps to master scoring:

  1. Pre‑heat and Prepare. Heat your oven to 475°F (245°C) with a Dutch oven inside. While it preheats, dust the baking sheet with a light coating of semolina or cornmeal to prevent sticking.
  2. Shape the Loaf. After the final rise, turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface. Use the dough scraper from the set to smooth the surface and cut a thin “slice” to shape the baguette’s classic taper.
  3. Score with the Lame. Hold the lame at a 45‑degree angle to the dough’s surface. Apply gentle pressure and glide the lame in a single, swift motion. For a baguette, a single long diagonal cut from the base to the tip works best. Repeat on the opposite side for symmetry.
  4. Final Touches. Lightly brush the loaf with water or a beaten egg for extra shine. Slide the baguette into the preheated Dutch oven, cover, and bake 20 minutes.
  5. Uncover and Finish. Remove the lid, lower the temperature to 425°F (220°C), and bake another 15‑20 minutes until the crust is deep golden brown.

Troubleshooting Common Scoring Problems

Even seasoned bakers hit snags. Here’s how to fix them:

  • Too Much Steam. If the loaf puffs up too quickly and collapses, your score was too shallow or too wide. Aim for a clean, single cut.
  • Uneven Crust. A ragged score can create uneven expansion. Use the lame’s smooth edge to keep cuts straight.
  • Sticking to the Pan. The dough may cling if the surface isn’t adequately floured. Sprinkle a bit more semolina or use parchment paper.

Beyond the Basics: Creative Scoring Ideas

Once you’re comfortable, experiment with patterns. A series of shallow slashes can create a rustic look, while a zig‑zag adds visual interest. Just remember that each cut is a potential expansion line—too many can cause the loaf to split in unintended ways.

Why the 3‑in‑1 Whisk Set is a Game‑Changer

The Sourdough Whisk Set streamlines the entire process. The Danish dough whisk’s flexible strands fold dough without deflating it, the scraper keeps the surface clean for crisp scoring, and the bread scoring lame is precision‑engineered for sharp, clean cuts. Having all three tools in one kit means you spend less time hunting for pieces and more time enjoying fresh bread.

FAQ

What temperature should I bake my sourdough baguette?

Preheat to 475°F (245°C) with a Dutch oven inside. After 20 minutes, reduce to 425°F (220°C) and bake until the crust is deep golden.

Can I use a regular knife instead of a lame?

While a knife can work, a lame provides a cleaner cut and less risk of tearing the dough. It’s especially helpful for beginners.

How do I keep the scored lines from closing during baking?

Score deep enough—about 1/4 inch into the dough—and brush the loaf with water before baking. This creates steam that keeps the cuts open and the crust crisp.
